pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, picture and bar graphs become SCALED: one square (or symbol) represents several units — 2, 5 or 10 — so reading and drawing now depend on the scale/key, on reading intermediate values (a half-symbol, a bar top between gridlines), and on solving one- and two-step comparison, sum and difference problems. This is the NC Year 3-4 step from single-unit to scaled representations. The core new demand is that height/length no longer equals count directly — it must be read THROUGH the scale. Teaching should make the scale explicit and chosen for the data, model reading intermediate values, and rehearse two-step problems as two separate reads-then-combine.
bestPractices: Read the scale/key first, every time ('each square stands for 5'), before reading any value
Choose a sensible even scale for the data when constructing (so the largest value fits and marks are equal), and connect it to multiplication/counting in that step
Model reading intermediate values — half a symbol is half the key; a bar top halfway between 10 and 15 is 12 or 13 depending on the scale
Break two-step problems into explicit steps: read each value, then decide and do the combine (sum or difference)
keyRepresentations: Scaled bar graph on squared paper (each square = 2/5/10)
Scaled pictogram with a stated key and part-symbols
Frequency table as the source, with the scale chosen from the largest value
Two bars aligned for a difference, or stacked for a sum
commonMisconceptions: Ignores the scale and reads each square/symbol as one unit (or just counts symbols)
Cannot read an intermediate value — rounds a mid-interval bar to a gridline or ignores a part-symbol
Collapses a two-step problem to one step (reads a value but doesn't combine, or does the wrong operation)
Constructs a scaled axis with unequal intervals, so positions no longer map to values

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, picture and bar graphs become SCALED: one square or symbol stands for several units (2, 5 or 10). The core new demand is that a bar's height or a row's length no longer equals the count directly — it must be read THROUGH the scale/key. Learners should read the key first every time, read intermediate values (a half-symbol = half the key; a bar top read by counting the sub-intervals between gridlines), choose a sensible scale (such as 2, 5 or 10) with equally spaced intervals when constructing, and solve one- and two-step comparison, sum and difference problems as explicit 'read each value, then combine' steps. This is the NC Year 3-4 step from single-unit to scaled representations.

activities.title: Flip the scale: watch the same bars change value
feedback: If a learner reads each square as one unit, have them read the key aloud first and re-read each value by multiplying by the scale (e.g. 3 squares at 'each square = 5' is 3 × 5 = 15).
If an axis is drawn with unequal intervals, point out that positions no longer map to values; redraw with equal spacing and connect each step to counting on by the scale.
When the scale flip is understood, prompt: 'you chose each square = 5 — why is that a good scale for this data?' to confirm the choice is owned, not copied.
activities.rationale: Making the scale selectable or re-labelled turns 'reading through the scale' into a felt action: the same bars mean different amounts as the key changes, which targets the misconception of reading each square as one unit. Choosing a scale connects the representation to multiplication/counting.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils interpret and present data using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables and solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' problems; non-statutory guidance specifies simple scales (2, 5, 10 units) with increasing accuracy
learnerActions: Draw bars for a small data set on squared paper where 'each square = 1'.
Then change the key to 'each square = 5' and re-read every bar: say what each bar now means (e.g. a 4-square bar is now 20, not 4).
State out loud: 'The height on its own doesn't tell me the value — I only know the value once I read it through the scale.'
Optional with an interactive scaled-graph builder: use a scale selector (each square = 2/5/10) that re-labels the axis live, so the same drawn bars instantly re-map to new values.
Choose a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) for a given data set so the largest value fits, mark the axis in equally spaced intervals, and explain why that scale works.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar's or symbol's size maps to a value only via the scale; changing the scale re-maps every value, and a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) makes the largest value fit with equal intervals.

activities.title: Reading values between the marks
feedback: If a half-symbol is read as a whole symbol, show that half a symbol equals half the key's value and re-read the row (e.g. half of a key of 10 is 5).

If a mid-interval bar is rounded to a gridline, have the learner count the sub-intervals of the scale between the two gridlines to find the in-between value, and state the exact value (including a half, e.g. 12½, when the bar lands at a midpoint).
activities.rationale: Intermediate reading is a distinct skill from reading marked points; isolating half-symbols and sub-interval bars targets the specific error of rounding to a gridline or ignoring a part-symbol. Using an even key keeps the learner-facing values exact rather than rounding a 2½.
sourceClaims: A pictograph uses a symbol to represent several items in a category (many-to-one), distinct from a picture graph's one-symbol-per-individual — the basis of reading a scaled key correctly
learnerActions: Read a scaled pictogram with a stated key (e.g. one symbol = 10 children) that includes half-symbols, and give the value of a row ending in a half-symbol: a half-symbol is half the key (with a key of 10 that is 5). Note that with a key of 5 a half-symbol is 2½, which is why pictograms are usually built with an even key so half-symbols land on whole numbers.

Read a scaled bar whose top reaches a specific sub-interval mark between two gridlines — e.g. a bar reaching the 13 mark between the 10 and 15 lines — and state its value by counting the scale's sub-intervals. Separately, note that a bar sitting exactly at the midpoint of 10 and 15 reads as 12½, not a whole number.
Optional with draggable part-symbols or a draggable bar top: hit an exact intermediate value and check it against the key by counting sub-intervals.
activities.intendedInsight: Part-symbols and bar tops between gridlines carry real values: a half-symbol is half the key, and you read between gridlines by counting the scale's sub-intervals rather than rounding to the nearest line.

activities.title: Two-step problems as two reads then combine
feedback: If a learner gives a single value for 'total of the top two', scaffold the two steps explicitly: read value one, read value two, then combine.
If a learner subtracts when a sum is needed (or vice versa), ask what the question is asking for — a total (add) or a difference (subtract) — before computing.
For 'how many more', watch for giving the larger value instead of the difference; prompt for the gap between the two readings.
activities.rationale: Separating the read step from the combine step directly addresses collapsing two-step problems to one step and choosing the wrong operation, the common performance errors at this stage.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils interpret and present data using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables and solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' problems; non-statutory guidance specifies simple scales (2, 5, 10 units) with increasing accuracy
learnerActions: From a scaled graph, answer a 'how many more' comparison (e.g. how many more chose football than tennis?) by reading each value through the key and finding the difference.
Solve a two-step problem such as 'how many altogether for the top two choices?' by first reading each of the two values separately, then deciding whether to add or subtract, then doing it.
Say the two steps aloud before answering: 'First I read these two values; then I [add/subtract] them.'
Optional with a question panel that shades each bar as it is read before combining, so the two reads are visible as two distinct actions rather than one glance.
activities.intendedInsight: The two-step data problems here are two reads followed by one combine (sum or difference); naming both steps helps prevent collapsing it to a single glance or using the wrong operation.

activities.title: Construct a scaled graph from a frequency table
feedback: If the chosen scale makes the largest value overflow the grid or produces awkward marks, prompt choosing a larger scale (e.g. moving from 2 to 5 or 10) so the biggest value fits.
If intervals are uneven, re-space them equally so each step up the axis adds the same amount.
Confirm ownership by having the learner read their own graph back through its scale and compare to the table.
activities.rationale: Producing a graph (not just reading one) exposes whether the scale idea is genuinely owned; choosing the scale and spacing intervals equally is where unequal-axis errors surface.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils interpret and present data using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables and solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' problems; non-statutory guidance specifies simple scales (2, 5, 10 units) with increasing accuracy
learnerActions: Take a frequency table (e.g. swimming 20, cycling 15) and choose a sensible scale that fits the largest value with equal intervals (e.g. each square = 5, giving 4 squares and 3 squares).
Draw the bars from the baseline with equal width, each reaching the correct scaled position.
Alternatively draw a scaled pictogram with a stated key, using a part-symbol where the value is not a whole multiple of the key.
Check: does each drawn bar/row read back to the original data value when read through the chosen scale?
activities.intendedInsight: Constructing a scaled graph requires choosing a workable scale from the data, keeping intervals equal and bars from the baseline, so that positions map back to the intended values.

constraints: Always read the key/scale first, before reading any value ('each square stands for 5').

Learners should both READ and CONSTRUCT scaled graphs; recognition-only or tap-to-reveal items that show a key and values can check reading but do not themselves elicit the independent scale choice or multi-step solving that construction and open problems require.
A static scaled graph with a tappable key can serve as a reference, but it cannot let the learner change the scale or solve multi-step problems; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
Multiple-choice two-step items should include a 'one-step' wrong option (just the top value) so collapsing to one step is detectable; such items check reading/solving but do not require construction.
Half-symbols and bar tops between gridlines must be included so intermediate reading is practised, not avoided.

When a half-symbol or mid-interval value is used with learners, choose a key/scale that yields an exact value (e.g. an even key so a half-symbol is a whole number), or state the half value explicitly (2½, 12½) rather than rounding to a nearby whole number.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' entries were marked poor fit with claims that dialogue 'supplies none' and '3D adds nothing'. These are not established as universal laws; discussion can support naming the two steps and choosing a scale, so talk prompts are retained within activities. The narrow objective point — flat scaled graphs do not require a 3D model, and learners need the graph itself to act on — is preserved as a scaffolding limit, not a universal claim about media.

With a key of 5, a half-symbol is exactly 2½; the original's '2 or 3' is a rounding choice, not a clean value. Learner-facing examples now use an even key (10) so a half-symbol reads as a whole number, and the 2½ case is stated explicitly rather than rounded.

A bar 'halfway between 10 and 15' is exactly 12½; the original '12 or 13' is only correct if the bar actually reaches the 12 or 13 sub-interval mark. The learner example now uses a single determinate sub-interval value, and the specific grid's sub-intervals should be checked before asserting a single whole value.
Mid-interval values such as 12½ do not occur for whole-count data; such examples illustrate the reading arithmetic rather than realistic discrete counts.

The source claims support the curriculum content (scaled charts with 2/5/10 scales; many-to-one pictograph keys) but do not establish that the proposed interactive scale-selector or any specific medium is necessary or more effective than another; efficacy is treated as intended, not demonstrated.

probeDeeper: Ask 'what does one symbol/square stand for here — how did you use that?' to check the scale is applied, not ignored
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'this bar reaches halfway between 10 and 15 — what value is that?' to test intermediate reading
Ask 'for the total of the top two, what two things do you have to do?' to surface the two-step structure
Ask 'you chose each square = 5 — why is that a good scale for this data?' to probe sensible scale choice when constructing
assess.correctAnswer: Interpreting: reads values THROUGH the key (symbols ×5, half-symbol = 2 or 3), and gives the difference for 'how many more'. Translating: draws bars for 20 and 15 using an even scale that fits (e.g. each square = 5), equal width from the baseline.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the scale/key and reads each symbol or square as one unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the key aloud first; overlay the count each symbol carries; re-read via multiplication by the scale
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads 3 football symbols as 3 rather than 15

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot read an intermediate value — rounds a mid-interval bar to a gridline or ignores a part-symbol
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show half a symbol = half the key; count the sub-intervals of the scale to read between gridlines
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads a half-symbol as a whole, or a bar halfway between 10 and 15 as 10 or 15

errorPatterns.pattern: Collapses a two-step problem to one step — reads the values but doesn't combine, or applies the wrong operation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two steps explicitly: read each value, then decide sum or difference and do it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a single value for 'total of the top two', or subtracts when a sum is needed

responseLevels.gap: Ignores the scale (reads as units), can't read part-values, and solves only single steps or draws uneven axes
responseLevels.full: Reads scaled and intermediate values via the key, solves two-step sum/difference problems, and constructs a scaled bar graph choosing a sensible even scale
responseLevels.partial: Reads scaled values at marked points and solves one-step problems, but misses intermediate values or the second step, or needs the scale chosen for them

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First: here is a scaled pictogram of favourite sports where one symbol stands for 5 children (and half-symbols appear) — how many chose football, and how many MORE chose football than tennis? Then: here is the data for two more sports (swimming 20, cycling 15) — draw them as bars on this grid, choosing a sensible scale.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with scaled-graph fluency reads via the key/scale, handles part-symbols, computes differences, and chooses a workable even scale when drawing; a child without it counts symbols as ones, ignores half-symbols, gives the larger value for 'how many more', or draws an uneven axis. The construct step exposes whether the scale idea is owned.
